media.title: Age 15 Joshua Aronson on Stereotype Threat

timecodes.what: Around kf_002.jpg (5.5s) (widescreen camera frame), speaker commentary notes "One other fragility factor, one that I am going to focus on for the rest of the time is this thing that we call stereotype threat.", anchoring the research context of two Stanford GRE test booklets side-by-side — identical inside, differing only by the Page-1 'Diagnostic Ability' vs 'Problem-Solving Puzzle' cover.

At kf_008.jpg (38.5s) (widescreen camera frame), audio continues with "Black students, on average, score about 100 points lower on the SAT than white students, the average. There's usually a standard deviation difference.", detailing experimental methodology and behavioral observations for Claude Steele & Joshua Aronson's 1995 Stanford GRE verbal framing & race-priming experiments.

Later widescreen camera frame at kf_010.jpg (49.5s) accompanied by "There's usually a standard deviation difference. Socioeconomics narrows the gaps, but it doesn't wipe it out completely.", summarizing mechanism and boundary conditions in Claude Steele & Joshua Aronson's 1995 Stanford GRE verbal framing & race-priming experiments.

media.title: Claude Steele on Stereotype Threat

timecodes.what: Lecture slide / diagram frame at kf_003.jpg (10.0s) paired with transcript segment "Stereotype threat is just the experience of being in a situation where you know that you could be judged or treated in terms of a negative stereotype", introducing core background on two Stanford GRE test booklets side-by-side — identical inside, differing only by the Page-1 'Diagnostic Ability' vs 'Problem-Solving Puzzle' cover.

Around kf_009.jpg (40.0s) (widescreen camera frame), transcript records "and distracting and it can interfere with your functioning right there. Just the tension caused by that. That's really what stereotype threat is.", examining procedural mechanics and evidence in Claude Steele & Joshua Aronson's 1995 Stanford GRE verbal framing & race-priming experiments.

At kf_011.jpg (50.0s) (widescreen camera frame), speaker remarks "That's really what stereotype threat is. In writing the book, I asked myself, well, "When did first realize I was Black?" When did I first become...", addressing theoretical interpretation and downstream implications of Claude Steele & Joshua Aronson's 1995 Stanford GRE verbal framing & race-priming experiments.
